extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narratology/literary theory; advanced creative-writing students and critical readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and analytic criteria for describing narrative description (types, framing, focalization, tropes such as ekphrasis/metaphor) and for diagnosing levels of narration (first/second-level narrators, embedded speech, signals of personal/impersonal language situations, text interference).

rubrics_metrics.name: The Metonymic Metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: The description is one large metaphor. The elements are contiguously related to one another. They form a coherent description that, taken as a whole, is the comparison of an object that is compared to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This relationship can remain implicit (in which case, out of context, it may be indistinguishable from other types). If an explicit comparing element appears, it produces a Homeric comparison. Use when elements form a contiguous, single-metaphor field.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Series of Metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: A description consisting of a metaphor that is expanded without continually referring to the compared element; the metaphor is repeatedly 'adjusted,' creating the impression that the compared element is elusive and indescribable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This rhetorical category characterizes certain historical styles; it produces a sense of elusiveness as the metaphor shifts and accumulates images rather than pinning down a referent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical novelistic description (introductory frame, subject–object split)
rubrics_metrics.description: A piece presenting itself as classical novelistic description: it comprises an introductory frame, a clear subject–object split, and a detailing of both the perception of the object and the elements constituting it, often uttered by an external narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for literalizing location phrases (e.g., 'On the second landing', 'On the bed'), an external narrator voice, and an organized detailing of the object's parts. This form tends to stop narrative momentum ('arrested') and foregrounds description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation (integration of description into narrative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Motivation: the subtle integration of the description into the narrative—how the act of perception is narrated so that description is motivated by narrative events or focalizer movement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify how the focalizer's movement (e.g., 'he goes up, then looks down') or narrative circumstances make the description plausible and embedded rather than gratuitous; motivated descriptions absorb into the narrative and can generate suspense or anticipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focalization and intensification of perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Focalization establishes the perceptual link between subject and object and can intensify perception (adding senses like sound and smell), expand the narrative moment, and prepare suspense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whose perception frames the description (external narrator, character-focalizer), whether perception is intensified (multisensory detail), and whether the moment is expanded/anticipatory to increase narrative importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ekphrasis and decentring evocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Ekphrasis: descriptive account of a (possibly non-existent) visual image; description can depart from strict referentiality by invoking other domains (painting, music, sea, forest), decentring the object into a domain of sense-perception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Note when description invokes other arts or imaginary images ('like a painting by the douanier Rousseau'); ekphrasis can interrupt narrative yet also constitute narrativity and complicate realist expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description as both narrative's 'other' and an integral part
rubrics_metrics.description: Description can be both interruption of narrative (non-narrative) and constitutive of narrative; it can produce characters and narrative time rather than simply report them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether description merely pauses story or actually generates character/time/expectation (e.g., producing the character for the narrative through extended metaphor), and how it negotiates realism and modernist subjectivity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordering principles of description
rubrics_metrics.description: Conventional orders for descriptions include: for persons, head-to-foot and centre-to-periphery; for landscapes, foreground-to-background or vague-to-clear; alternately, descriptions may run through the senses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether a text follows expected ordering (top→bottom, foreground→background, sight→smell→sound) or deliberately subverts the order (e.g., inserting smell early) to produce stylistic effects or to absorb description in narrative motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing / Delimitation (literalizing realist framing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Framing: introductory locative phrases and scene-setting devices that literalize a realist frame (e.g., 'On the second landing of the hotel…').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify framing clauses that set up a realistic viewpoint or painting-like frame; framing can naturalize description and align reader expectation with a realist tradition or, if ruptured, signal modernist strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signals of emotive language as level indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Emotive language (e.g., exclamations like 'Oh', exclamation marks, absence of verb) signals emotive function and can indicate a change in narrative level (embedded speech or thought).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence/absence of declarative/attributive verbs and punctuation to determine whether an emotive phrase is direct discourse, embedded speech/thought, or part of the narrator's voice; absence of a verb can strengthen emotional immediacy and indicate embedding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declarative verbs, quotation marks, colons/dashes as markers of embedded sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear change of narrative level is often indicated by a declarative verb, a colon, a dash, or quotation marks; these mark when a first-level narrator yields to a second-level speaker (embedded sentence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing a passage, treat verbs of saying, punctuation, and quotation marks as formal signals that the textual voice has shifted into direct speech or another narrative level (CN1[CN2] structures).

rubrics_metrics.name: Levels of narration taxonomy (NI(p), CN1, CN2, narrator-witness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinctions between narrator types and levels: second-level character-bound narrator (CN2); first-level character-bound narrator (CN1); perceptible narrator (NI(p))—signals indicate whether narrator is present/perceptible or merely reporting; narrator-witness is an internal narrator who functions as a witness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify who is speaking and at which level; determine whether quoted material belongs to an actor (CN2) or to the narrator (CN1), and whether the narrator is testifying/witnessing (implicating presence) or is external.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perceptibility of quoted speech/thought as a fictionality marker
rubrics_metrics.description: When an utterance narrated at the second level is not perceptible to other actors (only accessible to the reader), this non-perceptibility is an indication of fictionality and can violate a realistic rhetoric of 'testimony.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether quoted thoughts/speeches are audibly present to other characters; if not, the narrative is granting readers privileged access and may create strategic inequalities between characters and readers (used to effect in many novels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Text interference (mixture/merging of narrative levels)
rubrics_metrics.description: Text interference: when personal language situations intrude into impersonal ones (or vice versa), causing narrative levels to intertwine or merge (e.g., a perceptible narrator stepping into the second level or vice versa).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect instances where the narrator's self-reference or emotive language 'steps across' into character speech, or where actors' discourse is represented at the narrator's level—this signals blurring of narrative boundaries and can produce testimonial or irony effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signals distinguishing personal vs impersonal language situations (1–7)
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal vs impersonal language situations can be distinguished by textual signals: 1) personal pronouns; 2) grammatical person; 3) tense; 4) deixis (this/these, here/there, adverbs of place/time); 5) emotive words/aspects (oh!); 6) conative words/aspects (please, address/command/question); 7) modal verbs/adverbs indicating uncertainty (perhaps).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the numbered signal set to classify passages: personal = I/you, 1st/2nd person, not all past tenses possible, presence of 'this/here/today', emotive/conative language, modals marking speaker uncertainty; impersonal = he/she, 3rd person, all past tenses possible, that/those, absent deictics and emotive/conative markers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotive function implies self-reference
rubrics_metrics.description: If a statement expresses the speaker's feelings (emotive function), it is about the speaker and thus a sign of self-reference; such signs often indicate that an actor with the same identity as the narrator forms part of the fabula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When emotive words or constructions are present, consider whether the narrator is referring to its own language situation (perceptible narrator) and how that affects the balance of power and presence in the narrated world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect discourse and its tense/deictic shifts
rubrics_metrics.description: Indirect discourse: the narrator represents the actor's words rather than quoting them verbatim; such forms often involve backshifts in tense and deictic shifts (e.g., 'tomorrow night' → 'the following night').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for transformations of direct quotes into reported speech (examples h–k): check for modal/tense changes and shifting deictic expressions as indicators of the level at which the utterance is represented and of narrator mediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of narrative-level analysis as a tool for literary history/periodization
rubrics_metrics.description: The structure of levels of narration and forms of description can be used to characterize narratives historically (e.g., Flaubert's early internal narrator as realist device; Proust's subjective internal narrator as modernist), but should avoid facile categorizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply level-analysis to compare authors/periods, noting how specific uses (collective 'nous', 'I' as witness, quoted speeches, indeterminacy of addressee) contribute to period poetics while allowing for nuanced exceptions.
